abstract.p: Information retrieval systems often generate observations that are either finite unordered sets of documents, or finite prefixes of arbitrarily long ordered rankings of documents. To assess system quality those observations are then compared to corresponding reference sets or rankings to generate scores that measure how closely the observation achieves the target established by the reference. Recent work by Corsi and Urbano has considered Rank-Biased Overlap, a "ranking against ranking" measurement, and proposed an "expectation over permutations" mechanism to handle ties in rankings, where ties are groups of documents that are assigned the same importance. In this paper we note that ties in rankings arise in two complementary ways. The first is that the tied scores represent indecision on the part of the system, but that there is nevertheless a single underlying ordering, and hence that, to be informative, reported measurements should be inclusive of (as a lower bound) a "most disadvantageous" permutation, and (as an upper bound) a "most advantageous" permutation. The second option is that ties represent genuine equality, with all tied documents regarded as sharing the depths spanned by that tied group. We then argue that neither of these two interpretations of ties is fully resolved by the recent Corsi and Urbano proposal, and describe mechanisms that address that gap. To illustrate these ideas, we measure the consequences of the new and previous tie-breaking approaches using all of the runs from two TREC Web collections.
